div.head: One of the underestimates in schedulability analysis of a bus-based real-time multiprocessors is the impact of the system bus. The system bus is a source of schedulability loss caused by the bus interference as well as a shared resource. In this paper we first identify the impact factors of the system bus on schedulability as follows: management of the priorities of tasks at the bus interface and the bus arbitration policy. We then investigate the impact of the waiting time of each task required to use the system bus on the schedulability f o r different number of processors and various memory request rates. Analysis results based on a discrete time Markov chain show that when the memory request rate of each processor is less than IS%, ihe impact of the waiting time is negligible; otherwise, the waiting time must be taken into account in schedulability analysis. div.head: Introduction
div.p: The trend of next generation real-time systems is based on open systems which incorporate open architectures using off-the-shelf standard microprocessors, standard backplane bus, and standard realtime operating systems. The concept of open realtime systems reduces system cost, increases ease-ofuse, and enhances the flexibility of system integration [l]. Most of the recent real-time applications require huge amount of computation, which leads to the development of a popular open hardware ar- chitecture consisting of multiple standard processors sharing a common memory. A simple method for buildin shared memory multiprocessors is just to assembfe a collection of processors and the memory on a standard backplane bus. The bus-based multiprocessors allow application of parallel processing technique to a wide variety of practical applications including real-time applications. However, since all shared memory accesses have to go through the system bus, processors compete for the access to the system bus. As more processors are added and/or the memory access rate of each processor is high, their activity introduces delays which may slow all processors. In general purpose computing on a busbased multiprocessors, the amount by which each processor is slowed due to the bus contention ultimately degrades the performance of multiproces-Heonshik Shin Dept. of time computing where both the logical correctness of computation and the timely execution of tasks are required, the delay time caused by the bus contention affects the degree of resource utilization, that is, schedulability, at or below which the deadlines of real-time tasks can be guaranteed. In real-time systems which manage tasks based on priorities, a high priority may preempt a lower priority, and task interference or blocking arises when tasks share resources. This blocking is the additional time a task has to wait relative to the situation where there is no resource sharing. Resource sharing is a fundamental factor to be considered in the schedulability analysis of real-time systems. Blocking in uniprocessor system, called priority inversion, can be defined as the duration a task with a high priority has to wait for the execution of lower priority tasks [5]. In bus-based multiprocessors environment, the blocking can be caused by any task on other processors regardless of their priorities, which is the concept of remote blocking [6]. Even though the system bus in a bus-based multiprocessors is a source of blocking when the processors access shared memory and other shared resources, the impact of the blocking time on the schedulability analysis has drawn less attention than it should have in the previous studies [6] [q. If either the ratio of data-sharing is high or the number of processors is large, the waiting time of each task to access the bus must be added to the duration of blocking for accurate analysis of schedulability.

In this paper, we investigate the impact of the bus access time of each priority on the schedulability of real-time shared-bus multiprocessors. Section 2 describes a bus-based real-time multiprocessor model to be referenced to classify the impact factors of the system bus on schedulability. In Section 3, we compute the amount of waiting time for each priority level to access the s stem bus by using a discrete time Markov chain f8]. This section also reports the analysis results for schedulability loss for various memory request rates. Concluding remarks and suggestions for future works are given in Section 4.

In standard backplane buses such as Futurebus+ [9 and Multibus I1 [lo], the bus arbitration is primari I y based on the priorities of processors, and the physical identification number of processors when more than one processor are competing for the bus with the same priority.

In a real-time multiprocessors environment the priority at the transmission queue can be managed by priority overwrite [ll] or priority ceiling protocol [ 5 ] . For both cases, the priority for arbitration is determined by the priorities of the tasks allocated to a processor and the unique identification uumber assigned to each processor for fairness arbitration. When processors are competing for the bus with a priority, a processor with the highest priority is granted and the other processors are waiting until the bus is free. A bus request that is not satisfied is generally resubmitted. We define the bus access time Bburwait as the waiting time until a request successfully accesses the bus and it is measured in the bus arbitration cycle time t o r b . The t o r b amounts to the pure bus arbitration time including arbitration procedure, fairness check, and a winner decision. The amount of waiting time of each priority depends on both the bus arbitration policy and the frequency of bus requests of a processor for a shared memory access.

In the following, we assume that real-time tasks are bound to processors statical1 and scheduled by the Rate Monotonic Algorithm ill. In rate monotonic scheduling, the tasks with shorter periods have high priorities so that the execution of high priority tasks precede that of low priority tasks. The schedulability of a set of i tasks can be checked by the schedulability bound function U ( i ) , where i is the priority of each task with 1 for the highest priority, 2 for the next highest, and so on. U(? is composed of preemption term, execution term an blocking term. We also assume the period of task as millisecond which is typical in real-time applications such as air traffic control and scientific data acquisition [l].

div.head: Impact factors of system bus on
div.p: It is necessary to determine the worst case blocking time of each task for the schedulability analysis of real-time systems. In shared-memory real-time multiprocessors, the worst case blocking time of each task consists of the local processor blocking time and the interprocessor blocking time [13]. Local blocking is the time blocked by the lower priority tasks allocated to a processor, and depends on both the characteristics of the task set allocated on a processor itself and the management strategy of the priorities of tasks at the transmission queue. However, the nature of the interprocessor blocking is different from that of local blocking and makes the schedulability analysis of real-time multiprocessors difficult. Interprocessor blocking is the waiting time interferenced among processors, which is similar to the remote blocking conceptually. It depends on the characteristics of tasks allocated on other processors and the bus arbitration policy, particularly the mechanism of priority assignment to processors.

The following example demonstrates two factors of the system bus which have impact on the schedulability of real-time multiprocessor; (1) how to manage the task's priority at transmission queue of the bus interface unit(B1U) (2) how long a task has to wait under the given bus arbitration policy. For schedulability Table 1: An example task sets. analysis purposes, there are two cases to be considered depending on how to manage priorities at transmission queue. The goals of priority management at the transmission queue, such as priority overwrite and priority ceiling protocol, are to bound and/or minimize the blocking time of high priority tasks at local processor. Consider first the case when the priorities are managed by priority overwrite. In this case, the priority participating in bus arbitration is the highest priority of tasks queued for access to the system bus because the higher priority always overwrites the lower priority. For the above task sets, task r 1 has the highest priority because its period is the shortest and task rz has the lowest priority. Hence, the memory accesses of on Processor 1 can always precede the memory accesses of rz without local blocking. In the other case in which priorities are managed by the priority ceiling protocol, the priority of a processor participating in bus arbitration is the highest priority inherited from the priorities of tasks queued for transmission. As a result, there is local blocking due to the low priority tasks which arrive before the high priority tasks.

The interprocessor blocking arises when a processor competes for a shared memory access with a priority managed at the transmission queue. This blocking occurs even when the task's priority is managed by priority overwrite and results from two sources related to the bus arbitration: how to assign priorities to processors when more than one processor are competing for arbitration with the same priority and the delay time of each priority due to the priority based arbitration. Because of the above two interprocessor blocking sources, it is very cumbersome to determine the worst case execution time of each task. This difficulty is illustrated for the example task sets allocated to each processor in Table l. The priority of task r 3 is the same as that of r4 because two tasks have the same period. The memory accesses of r3 and r4 occur alternately according to fairness arbitration. A static task allocation strategy considering the interprocessor blocking was proposed [13], which assigns tasks to high physical identification priority processors in descending order of task priorities. Even though this task allocation strategy is independent of the interprocessor blocking, the waiting time required to access the system bus, which actually affects the schedulability of real-time tasks, cannot be eliminated because it is inherent to the multiprocessors system where processors share the system bus. For example, all memory accesses of r2 with the lowest priority, in the worst case, must wait for all memory accesses of all higher priority tasks. Thus the waiting time of 72, r3 and 74 except for the highest priority task TI to access the system bus must be taken into account for the blocking time of each task. div.head: Computation of waiting time
div.p: Each processor in the real-time shared-bus multiprocessors described in Section 2 participates in bus arbitration with a priority of tasks assigned to it regardless of the priority mangement schemes at the transmission queue. At any instant, the number of processors competing for the bus is at most the maximum number of processors installed in the system, which is tens of processor in the typical b u s based multiprocessor system. The priority distribution over processors for bus arbitration can be modeled as fixed priority levels assigned to each processor. The bus access time or waiting time of each priority level in fixed priority arbitration was analyzed by using a discrete time Markov chain [8]. By using the above Markov model the waiting time of each priority for different memory request rates P is computed in terms of the bus access time t a r ) , where all processors have the same memory request rate.

From Fig. 3 we can find that the amount of waiting time of each priority exponentially increases as the memory request rates increase, and the slope for high memory request rates becomes steeper. One interesting point to notice is the saturation point over which the waiting time barely increases for all request rates. The processor with a priority higher than the priority at the saturation point starves for the bus.

In the following, we consider only harmonic tasks for the simplicity of analysis because the priority assignment to each task and the periods of tasks can easily be computed. However, if the characteristics of a task set is known, the following analysis can be generalized for any task sets without restrictions. We assume the base period T of harmonic tasks as 1 msec [l] and tarb as 300 nsec [lo], which are typical in practice. Since typical units of the period of real-time tasks and the bus arbitration cycle time are msec and hundreds of nsec respectively, we can say that the cases in which the amount of waiting time is less than about 10,000 t a d have little effect on the schedulability. For the case in which the base period is 1 msec and tar) is 100 nsec, the S L due to the waiting time is 1%. Careful analysis of the waiting time for various memory request rates shown in Fig. 3 reveals that when T = 0.15 or less, the schedulability loss is under 3% which is negligible. When r > 0.15, the waiting time must be considered in the schedulability analysis as a part of blocking term. Fig. 4 shows the number of processors P supportable without schedulability violation versus the degree of schedulability loss for each number of processors. The schedulability violation means that, for any priority, the SL due to the waiting time to access the system bus is greater than 1. We can observe that the number of processors supportable without schedulability violation decreases as the memory request rates increase: for r = 0.16 P = 14, for r = 0.2 P = 11, for r = 0.25 P = 10 ,..., and for r = 0.30 P = 8. For the same number of processors supportable, the SI. for high request rates is greater than that for low rates. In the case of 10 processors, for example, SLs are 2.54% and 61.7% for r = 0.2 and r = 0.25, respectively. Table 2 shows that the impact of the waiting time on the schedulability boundary function U ( i ) which is the theoretical schedulability bound for a set of i tasks. U(;) is composed of preemption term, execution term and blocking term, where the blocking term is due to shared resources. The ratio % is a part of blocking term caused by sharing the system bus; it is often ignored in the schedulability analy- sis. For r = 0.2, the waiting time for the task with priority 11 to access the system bus takes 19.65% of its schedulability bound U(11). As the portion of the bus access time in the theoretical schedulability bound is larger, the probability that a task becomes unschedulable becomes higher. As a result, the schedulability loss becomes larger and less tasks are schedulable. The waiting time of each priority for the system bus is inherent to the bus-based realtime multiprocessor. It must be considered for exact schedulability analysis of real-time tasks.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We have analyzed the impact of the system bus on the schedulability of tasks in a bus-based real-time multiprocessors. The main goal of the analyses is to find out schedulability of real-time tasks by quantifying the blocking time that may occur while accessing the system bus. For analysis, two impact factors of the system bus on schedulability are identified: How to manage priority at the bus interface and the bus arbitration policy. The former is a source of local blocking and the latter is the source of interproces-5or blocking which is inherent to the multiprocessor environment.

From the computation of the mean access time for a bus using a discrete time Markov chain, we have shown that if the memory request rate of each processor is less than 16% the waiting time to access the bus is negligible, otherwise the waiting time should be considered for the schedulability analysis. We also present its impact on the mathematical schedulability bound for the harmonic tasks.

There are several directions in which the work presented here can be extended. One such direction is to further extend to the case in which tasks have independent periods. Another interesting direction is to integrate this blocking term into the timing tool for accurate schedulability analysis.
